passages.original: Siquidem de populo Judæorum fuerunt Prophetæ, per quos Evangelium, cujus fide credentes justificantur, ante promissum esse testatur : Segregatus enim, inquit, in Evangelium Dei, quod ante promiserat pcr Prophetas suos (Rom. I, 1, 2). Fuerum enim et prophetae non ipsius, in quibus etiam aliqua inveniuntur quae de Christo audita cecinerunt, sicut etiam de Sibylla dicitur : quod non facile crede- rem, nisi quod poetarum quidam in Romana lingua nobilissimus antequam diceret ea de innovatione sacculi, quae in Domini nostri Jesu Christi regnum satis concinere et convenire videantur, praeposuit versum, dicens : Ultima Cumæi veuit jam carminis aetas.
passages.english: For indeed the Prophets were from the people of the Jews, through whom he testifies that the Gospel, by faith in which believers are justified, was promised beforehand: "Set apart," he says, "for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his Prophets" (Rom. 1:1, 2). For there were also prophets not his own, in whom too some things are found which they sang [after] hearing [them] about Christ, as is also said of the Sibyl: which I would not readily believe, were it not that a certain poet, the most renowned in the Roman tongue, before he spoke those things about the renewal of the age which seem to harmonize and agree well enough with the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, set a verse before them, saying: "Now has come the last age of the Cumaean song."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "Fuerum" read as "Fuerunt", "pcr" as "per", "sacculi" as "saeculi", "veuit" as "venit". "Not his own" (non ipsius) presumably means prophets not belonging to God. The verse quoted is Virgil, Eclogue 4.4.
